doc.title: Dave Brubeck — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Broadway producers decline The Real Ambassadors
summary: Josh Logan and Leland Hayward liked the music, but the Broadway audience was not seen as ready for a show about integration.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Was there ever a thought of taking that to Broadway?

I did. I went away thinking I’m going to be recognized as a Broadway show writer, because one of the top guys that I took this to was so thrilled with the music I’d written. I remember he called his wife into the room and said, “Listen to this.” I played it for her and him again. That was Josh Logan. He sent one of his people in production up to Lenox School.

Oh. That was Leyland Hayward. So there’s two top names that were very interested. Then finally when it came time to not just interest, but putting up the money – I remember this session with them. They said, “Dave, the Broadway audience is not ready for a show on integration. You’ve got to remember that you’re lecturing to an audience that’s there to be entertained.” He made his point, that we were trying to – I wouldn’t call it lecture, but make people aware of the unfairness of segregation. They
came close to producing it, but said it wouldn’t work. Soon there was Raisin in the Sun, on Broadway.
Actually Raisin in the Sun predated that.
[ ]. We went to a reading of it.

Yes, and also another play that did not get on, that she wrote – I can’t think of her name at the moment – that Nemeroff was trying to produce. Yeah, I think it was difficult. That was – The Raisin in the Sun was a drama, and I think people expect a little more . . .

Yes. They’re willing to accept that, but in a musical – at that time, they expected a musical to be entertaining and not much else. It wasn’t until later that musicals started taking on a message, so to speak.
